rubric: Тезис поддержан точным анализом синтаксиса, иронии и образов.
Альтернативное прочтение содержательно и меняет возможный вывод.
Текстовые эффекты отделены от биографических причин.
Регистр, компрессия и устная реакция точны на уровне сложного профессионального общения.

tasks.prompt: Develop a close reading of two quoted passages, including one revision. Explain how syntax, irony or metaphor distributes agency; offer a plausible counterreading and mark the point where interpretation would become unsupported biography.
tasks.model: The committee “sufficiently distinguished to survive without meeting” turns status into a substitute for action: an apparently respectful institutional process absorbs the narrator’s request. Replacing “factory women” with “few officials” loses a specific account of users while sharpening the contrast between need and official experience. One could read this as broadening the satire rather than concealing inequality, but the effects can coexist. The timing of the typescript permits a question about the election; it does not establish electoral pressure or an authorial motive.
tasks.explanation: C2 требует анализа того, как именно язык производит смысл, с альтернативой, которую нельзя просто объявить ошибочной.

tasks.prompt: Reconstruct the strongest version of the historian’s and family representative’s positions. Identify the concession each accepts and explain the critic’s distinction between an interpretive argument and an exhaustive causal story.
tasks.model: The historian accepts that censorship is not established but argues that “universal” can obscure the significance of removed social detail. The family representative accepts conjecture if labeled but resists reducing Vale to a local dispute or treating aligned dates as a complete explanation. The critic can defend a reading of textual effects while refusing to claim that it explains every revision or the private intentions behind it.
tasks.explanation: Steelman обеих сторон должен сохранить их уступки, а не представить спор как политику против литературы.

tasks.prompt: Write a 400–520-word critical preface and an 80–120-word editorial note. Advance one nuanced thesis about silence, revision and power; analyze at least three precise textual choices; integrate a serious alternative; distinguish textual effect, attributed recollection and unproved motive. The note should tell readers how variants will be presented. Length is a genre guide, not an automatic score.
tasks.model:
PREFACE: Silence in Mara Vale’s essay is less the absence of speech than an institution’s capacity to make speech harmless. The opening grants that nobody is forbidden to speak, then withdraws the practical value of that freedom: sensible people are understood to have “already said enough.” The impersonal construction makes the rule difficult to locate. No official needs to issue it because reasonable membership in the town appears to require accepting it. The narrator’s request to repair a bridge is consequently met with language that honors concern while postponing action. A committee distinguished enough to survive without meeting turns prestige into a comic form of exemption. The joke is not simply that officials are idle; it is that the qualities used to authorize them also protect them from having to act.
The drafts complicate any account of this satire as either purely local or wholly universal. In one version, the bridge is the route factory women use before dawn. The published text instead identifies it as a route few officials need. Something is lost: workers’ gender, labor and daily movement become less visible. Something is also gained: official experience becomes the explicit measure of what the institution can fail to notice. These effects need not cancel each other. Nor must the earlier version be treated as an unfiltered truth against which publication is merely a retreat. The editor’s request to remove local particulars offers one account of the revision, but not an exhaustive explanation of its consequences.
The ending makes a related exchange. A direct question about the beneficiaries of delay gives way to agreement on “the importance of crossing,” while the river continues to cross whatever boundaries procedure imagines for it. Agreement becomes grammatically complete and practically empty. The river’s indifferent movement lends the satire an autonomy that a direct accusation might not possess. A counterreading is nevertheless worth keeping open: abstraction can make official evasion more durable as a target while making those who bear its costs harder to see.
Vale’s description of the revision as “less indictable and perhaps less innocent” refuses to settle the matter. It may suggest more elusive accusation, greater complicity or a sharper awareness of readers’ judgments. Her later resistance to a single identifiable mayor supports a broad institutional reading, but an author’s retrospective joke does not prohibit other well-grounded interpretations. The election near the typescript’s date supplies a possible research question, not a motive established by coincidence. Read together, the variants show silence being produced both within the town and around the text: what disappears can matter, without making disappearance the only story the archive tells.

EDITORIAL NOTE: Present the draft and published passages side by side, with dates and document types clearly identified. Distinguish changes visible in the texts from explanations offered in correspondence or later interviews. Do not label the draft “original truth” or the published version “censored” unless new evidence justifies those descriptions. Note that the archive contains no reply to Vale’s letter to her friend; that absence does not establish that the friend never answered. The introduction’s interpretation should remain separable from the transcription so readers can test its claims against the wording and pursue a different reading.
tasks.explanation: Модель делает тезис и анализирует устройство иронии. Альтернатива реально меняет оценку абстракции, а не служит декоративной оговоркой.

tasks.prompt: Record a 3–4-minute editorial defense. Historian: “Your elegant ambiguity lets the editor off the hook.” Distinguish accountability for visible choices from unproved motive. Family representative: “If Mara rejected local readings, why entertain one?” Respond, make one concession to each, then propose a sentence both could reasonably accept.
tasks.model:
To the historian, I would first say that naming uncertainty does not remove responsibility for a visible editorial choice. The factory women disappear from the published sentence. An introduction that calls this merely universal would repeat that disappearance by treating the people as expendable detail. I accept your concern, and I would keep the two formulations close together so readers can see exactly what changed.

What the record does not give us is a complete explanation of that change. The editor recommends removing local particulars, but we cannot turn a recommendation into proof of every private intention behind the finished text. The nearby election invites further research; it does not establish electoral pressure. We can criticize an effect without supplying an unsupported biography of its cause. That distinction makes the criticism more precise, rather than harmless.

I would also resist describing the published sentence only as a loss. By changing the focus to officials who rarely need the route, it makes a failure of institutional attention explicit. That does not restore the workers’ particular situation, but it creates a different contrast. My interpretation should show both consequences and explain why the social detail remains important. Otherwise, ambiguity would become a way of avoiding judgment instead of making a better one.

To the family representative, I accept that Vale resisted being reduced to a local quarrel. The preface should quote that resistance accurately and avoid treating the narrator as Vale speaking directly about an identifiable mayor. A later interview is nevertheless part of the evidence readers interpret, not an instruction that makes earlier variants irrelevant. Vale’s own joke about a more durable office encourages a broad institutional reading while leaving us to examine how that reading was made.

The same care applies to the ending. The river gives the published passage a force the direct question did not have. We should not treat revision as a simple movement away from truth, or assume that every gain compensates for a loss. Readers can test our account against the versions.

I propose this shared sentence: “The revision makes official indifference more explicit while reducing the visibility of particular bridge users; the archive documents those effects more securely than it documents the motives behind them.” Would both of you accept that as the starting point, even if you would give the two effects different weight?
tasks.explanation: Устный результат требует удержать несколько ходов аргумента и найти точную общую формулировку, не стирая разногласие.

tasks.prompt: Write a 140–190-word Russian introduction for an audio guide, then two English sentences for the technical catalog. Keep the audio accessible and the catalog evidentially exact; preserve the central interpretive dispute without importing your entire essay.
tasks.model:
В эссе Мары Вейл никто прямо не запрещает говорить. Вместо этого город превращает слова в безопасный ритуал: просьбу починить мост отправляют комитету, которому престиж позволяет не собираться. Черновик и публикация показывают, как меняется эта сатира. В черновике по мосту идут работницы фабрики до рассвета; в публикации это дорога, почти не нужная чиновникам. Конкретные люди становятся менее заметны, зато равнодушие власти звучит прямее. Можно видеть здесь расширение сатиры, но это не отменяет потери важных социальных подробностей.

Меняется и концовка. Прямой вопрос о выгоде от промедления уступает место реке, продолжающей движение, пока люди согласовывают важность перехода. Это художественный выигрыш, который не обязан компенсировать каждую потерю. Переписка помогает обсуждать изменения, однако не доказывает, что близкие выборы объясняют все правки. Позднее интервью тоже важно, но не запрещает читателю собственное обоснованное прочтение. Не стоит считать рассказчика прозрачной копией писательницы, а самый ранний вариант — единственной правдой. Сопоставьте версии и спросите, что каждая позволяет увидеть и что оставляет за пределами внимания.

The marked typescript predates a municipal election by two weeks; no supplied document identifies that election as a cause of revision. The edition distinguishes textual variants, contemporary correspondence and retrospective interview statements.
tasks.explanation: Посредник меняет плотность и регистр, но сохраняет различие эффекта, гипотезы и документированного факта.

transfer.prompt: A fictional poet changes “the nurses waiting for the night bus” to “those for whom the city stayed awake.” A publisher calls this universalization; a later interview rejects “reading poems as petitions.” Write a 250–350-word critical commentary with a real counterreading, and a two-sentence catalog note that does not infer censorship from the change alone.
transfer.model:
COMMENTARY: The revision changes both who waits and what the city appears to do. “The nurses waiting for the night bus” identifies workers, a practical journey and a schedule beyond the ordinary day. Waiting gives those workers an activity without giving them much control over it. The wording does not itself prove why the bus is needed or whether the service is inadequate, but it locates the experience in a recognizable working life.

“Those for whom the city stayed awake” removes the occupation and the bus. In their place, it gives the city an almost personal capacity to remain awake for someone. The phrase might sound generous: the city keeps something available when others are asleep. It might also suggest observation or a system that never allows some people to rest. These are possible effects of the wording, not facts about the city or the poet’s intentions.

I find the exchange productive but costly. The second version creates a wider field of association while making the original labor situation harder to see. A serious counterreading would give that openness more weight: readers with different night schedules could enter a phrase that no longer identifies one profession. That gain need not be dismissed as concealment. Equally, a publisher’s label of universalization should not make the lost specificity seem trivial.

The later objection to treating poems as petitions supports attention to form rather than a demand for a simple policy message. It does not settle how social meaning works in either version. Read together, the variants make us examine what abstraction enables and whom it may leave less visible, without requiring a story of censorship that the supplied evidence cannot establish.

CATALOG NOTE: The supplied versions replace a reference to nurses waiting for a night bus with a phrase about the city staying awake for unnamed people. The publisher’s description and the later interview are attributed interpretations; no supplied evidence establishes censorship as the cause of the change.
transfer.explanation: Новый образ допускает несколько функций; применить тезис о чиновниках без нового анализа недостаточно.

units.reflectionPrompt: Перепиши самый сильный и самый уязвимый абзацы предисловия. По-русски объясни, какая правка изменила аргумент, какая — ритм или подтекст и какую альтернативу ты теперь учитываешь честнее. Приведи исходные и новые ключевые фразы.

units.title: Разработать стандарт с честными границами
units.why: Согласуй нормативный текст, который остаётся исполнимым при неоднозначных понятиях и не превращает удобный показатель в цель.

materials.title: Письменные материалы
materials.text:
STANDARDS COMMITTEE DOSSIER — original fictional material.
An international consortium is drafting a voluntary standard for “meaningful human review” of automated recommendations in public-facing services. The current clause reads: “A qualified person shall review every consequential recommendation before action is taken.” A note defines consequential as “likely to materially affect an individual’s opportunities, access or treatment.” The draft does not define qualified, review or materially. Supporters say that flexible language allows organizations to apply the standard across sectors. Critics argue that a reviewer who sees only the system’s score and has thirty seconds per case may satisfy the clause on paper while being unable to challenge the recommendation.
A large provider proposes measuring compliance by the percentage of recommendations with a recorded human approval. In its pilot, 98.7 percent received such approval. Reviewers changed 0.4 percent, but the provider does not know whether the low change rate reflects high system quality, excessive trust, lack of time or limited access to evidence. A smaller organization uses a sampling process and escalates disputed cases. It cannot afford pre-action review of every recommendation and warns that a universal requirement could drive it out of the consortium. A service-user panel responds that affordability is relevant but cannot itself establish adequate protection. Panel members also distinguish a reviewer’s ability to disagree from an affected person’s ability to understand and contest a decision.
The committee must produce a core clause, guidance and a conformance statement that purchasers can read without specialist knowledge. Certification will initially assess documented processes and selected case records, not every real-world outcome. Some members want the label “human-verified decisions.” Others propose “process assessed against review requirements.” Marketing representatives object that the latter is less attractive. The consortium has not adopted a standard yet, and the fictional draft should not be treated as law or current industry guidance.
A technical annex suggests recording the information available to reviewers, time constraints, reasons for agreement or disagreement, escalation routes and the effect of a challenge on the final action. A privacy adviser warns that collecting full case narratives indefinitely may create a separate risk. An auditor notes that requiring reasons for every unchanged recommendation can produce boilerplate that looks substantial but conveys little. The committee has authority to require documented retention limits, access controls and proportionate sampling, but has not agreed exact durations or sample sizes. It must decide which obligations belong in the normative clause and which examples belong in guidance. Your task is not to eliminate every ambiguity. It is to make responsibilities, limits and routes for contestation explicit enough that implementation and criticism become possible.
materials.source: Авторский вымышленный материал English Workshop, 2026

materials.title: Сообщение / разговор
materials.text: Chair: We have a sentence everyone likes because everyone can imagine their own practice satisfying it. That is not necessarily consensus. Provider: Nor is a standard useful if it specifies an ideal process nobody can operate at scale. Panel member: Then name the tradeoff. Don't call a thirty-second rubber stamp meaningful because the alternative costs more. Small organization: We are asking for proportionate review, not permission to ignore people. Could risk-based sampling be legitimate if disputed cases are paused and independently escalated? Auditor: Potentially, but the standard must say what sampling can and cannot demonstrate. A high approval rate tells me that a button was pressed. It doesn't tell me whether the reviewer had a realistic basis to disagree. Privacy adviser: And a demand for richer evidence should not silently become a demand to retain everyone’s personal history forever. Marketing representative: “Process assessed” will sound evasive beside a competitor’s “human-verified.” Chair: It is less reassuring because our assessment is less comprehensive than that phrase implies. We should not borrow confidence from an outcome we have not examined. Panel member: Please keep contestation separate from internal review. Someone may need to challenge a decision even when a competent reviewer agreed with it. Provider: Would we have to publish every case rationale? Privacy adviser: No. We can require an intelligible explanation to the affected person while limiting public disclosure and internal retention. Auditor: The difficult part is checking that reasons are useful rather than decorative. We may need to inspect a sample and follow the path from concern to action, not merely count completed fields.

rubric: Нормативный текст исполним, внутренне согласован и отделён от примеров.
Показатели не подменяют содержательную цель.
Компромисс явно описывает остаточный риск.
Несколько жанров и аудиторий получают точное описание объёма уверенности.

tasks.prompt: Identify three ambiguities in the clause, distinguish review from contestation, and explain why neither a 98.7% approval rate nor a 0.4% change rate establishes meaningful review.
tasks.model: Qualification, access to evidence and the threshold of material effect are unspecified; “review” also lacks an operational account. Internal review concerns how an organization checks a recommendation, while contestation concerns an affected person’s ability to understand and challenge the resulting decision. Approval counts record process events; low modification could reflect accurate recommendations or ineffective scrutiny. Neither resolves the conditions under which disagreement was possible.
tasks.explanation: C2 требует различить конструкты и наблюдаемые следы, сохраняя несколько причин одного показателя.

tasks.prompt: Analyze the chair’s opening and the marketing exchange as arguments about apparent consensus and borrowed assurance. Reconstruct the small organization’s proposal without reducing it to cost avoidance.
tasks.model: The chair suggests that agreement on an undefined sentence may conceal incompatible implementations. Marketing seeks reassurance associated with verified outcomes even though certification inspects processes and samples. The small organization proposes proportionate sampling combined with pauses and independent escalation for disputes; its claim is conditional legitimacy, not that lower cost alone justifies weaker protection.
tasks.explanation: Подтекст связан с институциональной функцией формулировки, а не просто с нечестностью отдельного участника.

tasks.prompt: Draft a 130–180-word normative clause, 220–280 words of implementation guidance and a 60–90-word conformance statement. Define minimum review conditions, proportionate alternatives, contestation, evidence/retention limits and what certification does not establish. Explain one deliberate ambiguity in a short editorial note.
tasks.model:
NORMATIVE CLAUSE: An organization shall define which recommendations require review before action, using documented criteria for potential effects on individuals. Reviewers shall have relevant competence, access to the evidence needed to assess the recommendation, sufficient time and authority to question, change or escalate it. Where proportionate sampling replaces review of every case, the organization shall justify the scope and limitations of that approach and provide a route for disputed consequential cases to be paused and independently escalated before irreversible action. Affected individuals shall receive an intelligible explanation and an accessible route to contest the decision, including decisions previously approved by a reviewer. The organization shall retain evidence sufficient to assess whether these conditions operate in practice, subject to documented access controls and retention limits. It shall assess the usefulness of recorded reasons and the handling of challenges, rather than treating completion rates as sufficient evidence of meaningful review.

GUIDANCE: A reviewer’s approval is an event, not by itself evidence of substantive scrutiny. Evaluation should therefore examine what information was available, what constraints applied and whether a disagreement could change the outcome. A low change rate may be consistent with accurate recommendations, but may also indicate excessive trust or inadequate time. Organizations should investigate the context rather than set a target modification rate that encourages artificial disagreement. Sampling plans should explain which risks are covered and which remain outside their scope. A smaller provider may use a proportionate approach, but affordability does not remove the need for a credible escalation path. Internal review and individual contestation serve different purposes: a person may identify missing context after an otherwise competent review. Explanations should help the person understand and challenge the decision without requiring public disclosure of sensitive case details. Evidence collection should be limited to what is needed for accountability, with controlled access and justified retention periods. Auditors can inspect selected cases and trace a challenge through to action to assess whether reasons are informative or merely boilerplate. The standard does not prescribe one sample size or retention duration for every setting; organizations must justify those choices against the purpose, consequences and information involved. Guidance examples should remain distinguishable from mandatory requirements. A review team should be able to explain which requirement supports each requested record and how that record helps assess an actual decision path.

CONFORMANCE STATEMENT: This organization’s documented review process and selected case records have been assessed against the consortium’s review requirements. The assessment examines conditions for review and contestation within its stated scope. It does not verify every recommendation or guarantee that each resulting decision is correct. The assessment scope, sampling limitations and unresolved findings are available with this statement for purchasers to examine before relying on the claim.

EDITORIAL NOTE: “Sufficient time” remains context-dependent, but it is tied to available evidence and effective authority. A universal duration could reward compliance with a clock rather than the capacity to review.
tasks.explanation: Нормативный жанр задаёт обязанности; guidance объясняет применение; маркировка описывает реальный объём проверки, не заимствуя доверие от полного результата.

tasks.prompt: Record a 3–4-minute negotiation. Provider: “You are regulating judgment with paperwork.” Distinguish auditable conditions from guaranteed judgment and concede a genuine burden. Panel: “Sampling means some people get no protection.” Explain the limitation, offer a safeguard and ask what residual risk they consider unacceptable. End with a jointly usable clause revision.
tasks.model:
To the provider, I agree that a standard can create paperwork without improving judgment. A long explanation copied into every unchanged case would give an auditor more text and perhaps less useful evidence. I would not require that. The genuine burden includes staff time, decisions about sensitive information and the cost of making records accessible to reviewers. Those costs belong in our discussion.

However, removing the records would not make the underlying question disappear. We need to know whether a reviewer had enough information, relevant competence and actual authority to disagree. A checked box cannot establish those conditions. Nor does a low modification rate tell us whether the system was good or the review ineffective. We should inspect selected decision paths and ask what happened when someone raised a concern, rather than reward either agreement or disagreement as an outcome in itself.

To the panel, sampling does leave some cases without individual pre-action review. We must say that plainly. It cannot be marketed as a human verification of every decision. At the same time, a process can provide protections beyond that single stage: clear criteria for consequential cases, explanations to affected people and an accessible way to challenge a decision even when a reviewer originally agreed.

For disputed consequential cases, I propose a pause and independent escalation before irreversible action. The organization should also identify categories where the potential consequences make sampling unacceptable and require individual review there. Which categories would the panel put in that group, and what evidence would it need to accept sampling elsewhere? I am asking for a boundary we can implement and examine, rather than assuming that affordability settles it.

We also need to keep privacy in view. Richer evidence does not justify indefinite retention of complete personal histories. Access and retention limits should be documented, and reasons should be assessed for usefulness. A purchaser should see the scope and limitations of the process assessment, not a label suggesting certainty about every result.

My proposed revision is: “The organization shall identify consequential categories requiring individual pre-action review, justify any sampling used elsewhere, and pause disputed consequential cases for independent escalation before irreversible action.” That sentence leaves room to debate the categories while making the responsibilities visible. Would it address the provider’s concern about unnecessary records and the panel’s concern about protection being lost inside a percentage?
tasks.explanation: Устное владение проявляется в адаптации предложения после возражения и точном обозначении остаточного риска.

tasks.prompt: Write a Russian purchaser-facing explanation of the proposed label, followed by a short English implementation note for a small provider. Neither should imply that the standard exists or that compliance eliminates error.
tasks.model: Предлагаемая маркировка означает проверку описанного процесса и выборочных дел, а не подтверждение правильности каждого решения. Нужно смотреть область проверки, ограничения выборки и нерешённые замечания. Участие человека само по себе не доказывает содержательный контроль: важны информация, время, полномочия и путь оспаривания. Стандарт пока обсуждается. For a smaller provider, document why sampling is proportionate, what it cannot cover and how disputed consequential cases are paused and escalated. Do not use a process assessment to advertise every decision as human-verified.
tasks.explanation: Посредничество переводит техническую осторожность в полезное покупателю действие — изучить область и ограничения.

transfer.prompt: A consortium drafts a “sustainability-verified” label based on supplier questionnaires and a sample of site visits. Some small suppliers lack reporting teams; independent complaints reveal missing information. Write a clause, label and negotiation response that separate evidence, process and outcome without treating small size as either exemption or guilt.
transfer.model:
PROPOSED CLAUSE: A participant shall state which environmental claims its evidence supports and identify the limits of questionnaires and sampled site visits. It shall provide a documented route for independent complaints to trigger proportionate review and correction of unsupported claims. Reporting arrangements may be simplified for smaller suppliers, but reduced administrative capacity shall not by itself establish either conformance or nonconformance.

PROPOSED LABEL: Specified reporting processes and sampled supporting evidence have been assessed within the published scope. This assessment does not verify every supplier statement or guarantee every environmental outcome. Purchasers should consult the scope, outstanding findings and complaint-review arrangements.

NEGOTIATION RESPONSE: I accept that detailed forms can impose a disproportionate burden on a small supplier. We can provide simpler reporting support while retaining evidence for the actual claim. Where an independent complaint identifies missing information, could we require a targeted check and a clearly recorded response before repeating the disputed claim? That addresses the gap without presuming guilt from company size or treating a completed questionnaire as a verified outcome.
transfer.explanation: Новый предмет сертификации требует нового состава доказательств при сохранении честной границы маркировки.

materials.title: Письменные материалы
materials.text:
EDITORIAL PACKET — original fictional material.
A city magazine is debating a proposal to replace the last staffed ticket office at its central station with machines and remote video assistance. The transit authority says only 6 percent of tickets are now bought at the office. That figure excludes requests for route advice, help after service disruption and assistance with inaccessible payment interfaces. The authority estimates annual savings of $420,000, of which $110,000 would fund remote support. It has not costed additional station staff time if passengers ask platform workers for help. A three-week machine trial recorded a 94 percent transaction-completion rate among users who began a purchase; it did not count people who approached a machine and left without starting. The trial occurred outside the busiest holiday period. The authority has promised accessible interfaces but has not published the results of user testing.
An opinion columnist submits the following opening: “Progress has at last discovered a way to abolish the queue: abolish the person who notices you are in it. The machine, unlike the clerk, will never take a lunch break. It will also never notice that your carefully purchased ticket goes to a city you cannot reach because the connecting train was canceled. Such noticing is not, strictly speaking, a transaction, which may explain its unfortunate absence from the business case.” Later the column concedes that staffed offices can be inconvenient, inconsistent and intimidating. It argues that the relevant question is not whether machines are bad but which forms of help become invisible when success is defined as completed purchases.
A response from the authority calls the column “nostalgic resistance to modernization” and emphasizes that most passengers already choose digital tickets. A disability advocacy group supports better machines but wants the office retained until independent testing demonstrates that alternatives work for a range of users. A commuter association says closure could be acceptable if savings improve service and assistance is reliably available. Its spokesperson adds that permanent retention should not be assumed merely because the alternative is currently under-specified. The magazine’s editor wants an editorial that takes a position, evaluates the business case and treats these disagreements seriously. The editor does not want equal space mechanically assigned to every claim, nor a satire that converts uncertain consequences into established facts.
A late document clarifies that the $420,000 figure is gross savings before the remote-support cost. The authority has not yet specified whether video support will operate whenever trains run or only during office hours. It says it will answer questions before the final vote, which is six weeks away. The magazine has room for a 450-word editorial and a short social post. Your response may recommend conditional closure, temporary retention or another defensible option, but it must distinguish a demand for adequate evidence from a demand that change carry no risk. Use only the supplied fictional facts.
materials.source: Авторский вымышленный материал English Workshop, 2026

materials.title: Сообщение / разговор
materials.text: Editor: The opening is sharp, but does it imply that a machine can never help after a cancellation? Columnist: It exaggerates to expose what the metric misses. I can revise the absolute claim without giving up the point. Authority representative: If 94 percent complete purchases, focusing on edge cases seems disproportionate. Access adviser: That denominator begins after someone starts. It cannot tell us about people excluded before the first screen. Commuter representative: I agree, but we should not make the office immortal by defining success as perfect access for everyone. Editor: Then what would count as enough to change your mind? Access adviser: Published testing with people who face different barriers, a plan for disruption and clear support hours. Commuter representative: And a full cost comparison, including work shifted to platform staff. Authority representative: We can provide more detail, but independent testing could delay savings. Columnist: A delay has a cost; so does discovering after closure that the apparent savings were displaced onto passengers and other staff. Editor: That is the tradeoff. I want the editorial to state which uncertainties are decision-critical and which can be monitored after implementation. Access adviser: Please also avoid describing everyone who needs help as technologically incapable. People may be confident users and still face a canceled train or a payment failure. Commuter representative: And acknowledge that some people prefer machines precisely because human interactions have not always served them well.
materials.source: Авторский сценарий для синтезированной озвучки English Workshop, 2026

rubric: Риторика точна, сильна и не создаёт ложных фактов.
Обе сильные позиции представлены с уступками.
Числа, стоимость и знаменатели исправлены.
Позиция имеет реальное условие пересмотра и переносится в короткие жанры.

tasks.prompt: Analyze the satirical opening’s mechanism and limits, audit both percentages and calculate the currently identifiable net saving. Identify two missing costs or operating conditions that could change the recommendation.
tasks.model: The satire exposes a metric’s exclusion by treating the disappearance of human recognition as an efficiency gain. Its absolute claims risk overstating what machines cannot do. Six percent counts ticket purchases, not all assistance; 94 percent excludes people who never started a transaction. Identifiable savings after remote support are $310,000, before uncosted transferred work. Support hours, disruption arrangements, access testing and platform-staff workload could materially change the decision.
tasks.explanation: C2 объединяет риторическую точность с количественной: 420,000 − 110,000, но это ещё не окончательная чистая выгода.

tasks.prompt: Reconstruct the strongest closure-friendly position and the strongest retention-until-testing position. Explain how the editor distinguishes decision-critical uncertainty from a demand for perfect access.
tasks.model: The closure-friendly position accepts current gaps but argues that offices also impose costs and access failures, so retention should not become permanent by default. The testing position accepts improved machines but requires evidence and support arrangements before an irreversible reduction in assistance. The editor asks which unknowns could invalidate the design before closure, while allowing lesser problems to be monitored afterward rather than requiring zero risk.
tasks.explanation: Уступки обеих позиций существенны: без них получится ложная поляризация.

tasks.prompt: Write a 400–480-word editorial and a 45–65-word social post. Take a position, analyze a serious counterargument, integrate the late cost clarification, revise one satirical idea without a false absolute and specify a decision threshold plus post-change monitoring. The social post must preserve the core condition and avoid clickbait certainty.
tasks.model:
EDITORIAL: A ticket office does more than sell tickets, which is an awkward fact for a business case built around ticket sales. The proposal to close the central station’s last staffed office should therefore remain on hold until the authority publishes a complete assistance plan and a credible test of its alternatives. That is a condition for a decision, not a vote to preserve the counter forever. Machines can be convenient, consistent and preferable to an uncomfortable interaction. The columnist is right to ask what a transaction metric fails to notice, but the argument does not require pretending that a machine can never offer useful help. It requires asking whether the whole service will recognize problems that do not begin as purchases.
The authority’s figures are narrower than its reassurance. Six percent of tickets are bought at the office, but route advice, disruption support and failed payment interfaces are outside that count. The trial’s 94 percent completion rate begins only when a user starts a transaction. People who approach and leave before the first screen are absent, as is the pressure of the busiest holiday period. Neither figure proves that closure will fail; neither establishes that the replacement is adequate.
The financial case also needs its denominator. The advertised $420,000 saving is gross. After $110,000 for remote support, $310,000 remains before any additional work passed to platform staff. That could still be a substantial saving. Calling it illusory would be as premature as treating it as final. What matters is whether the proposed service can deliver that saving without quietly moving costs onto people who cannot obtain help.
Before the vote, the authority should publish support hours, arrangements for disruptions, user-testing results across relevant barriers and a cost comparison that includes transferred staff work. Independent scrutiny should test whether assistance remains usable when a routine purchase becomes an unusual problem. A requirement for perfect access would make any change impossible; a requirement to demonstrate how foreseeable failures will be handled is more modest and more necessary. If those conditions are met, conditional closure could be justified, with clear review points and a practical way to restore or expand in-person support. Monitoring should include abandoned attempts, unresolved requests and staff workload, not merely successful purchases. If the evidence is not ready in six weeks, the vote should wait. Delay has a price, but so does removing a service before understanding the work it performs. Modernization deserves a business case that counts that work, rather than defining it out of existence.

SOCIAL POST: Closing the ticket office may save money, but the current figures exclude some assistance needs and shifted staff costs. Our editorial supports a decision after published access testing, clear support hours and a complete cost comparison—not automatic permanent retention or closure. Successful purchases alone cannot show whether the replacement service works.
tasks.explanation: Редакционная позиция ясна, но условие изменения реально. Короткий пост сохраняет условие вместо рекламного преувеличения.

tasks.prompt: Record a 3–4-minute editorial defense. Authority: “You have made six percent of users veto everyone else.” Correct the category error and address proportionality. Columnist: “Your careful version has no teeth.” Defend a sharper but supportable line. Then state what evidence would change your position.
tasks.model:
Six percent is not the proportion of people who might need help. It is the proportion of tickets bought at the office, and the authority’s own measure leaves out route advice and support after disruptions. A confident machine user may still need help when a connecting train is canceled. We should not describe that person as technologically incapable, or treat a purchase count as a map of every service need.

I agree that proportionality matters. A small group should not acquire an automatic veto merely because it prefers the current arrangement. Staffed offices can also be inconvenient, inconsistent or intimidating, and machines may improve some experiences. Our position must compare functions, costs and alternatives rather than presume that human contact is always better. That is why I am proposing a condition for closure, not permanent retention by default.

The machine trial gives useful but limited information. Its ninety-four percent completion rate concerns people who began a purchase. It excludes those who left before starting, and it did not test the busiest holiday period. Those limits do not prove failure. They mean we need evidence about the people and conditions outside the measured transaction before using the result to justify the whole replacement.

To the columnist, careful language can still have teeth. I would use this line: “The business case may save the cost of the counter while leaving the work of the counter uncounted.” It identifies the problem without claiming that a machine can never help or that every proposed saving is imaginary. The late document makes the arithmetic clearer: four hundred twenty thousand dollars is gross savings; after remote support, three hundred ten thousand remains before additional platform-staff work has been costed. That could still be worthwhile.

I would change my position if published access testing, clear support hours, disruption arrangements and the full cost comparison show that the replacement can perform the necessary work. Independent scrutiny should include people facing different barriers, not only successful routine users. After any change, we should monitor abandoned attempts, unresolved requests and transferred workload, with a workable route to expand or restore in-person support.

If the evidence is ready before the vote in six weeks, conditional closure could be justified. If it is not, delay would carry a cost we should acknowledge openly. I would ask the authority which of these decision-critical questions it can answer before the vote, and ask the columnist to direct the satire toward the missing work rather than an unsupported absolute.
tasks.explanation: Ответ должен исправить ложный знаменатель и одновременно признать принцип соразмерности.

tasks.prompt: Produce a 140–180-word Russian briefing for a commuter forum and a two-sentence English correction for the magazine’s infographic. Preserve the position’s conditionality and label the savings accurately.
tasks.model:
Редакция предлагает отложить решение до проверки альтернатив, а не оставить кассу навсегда. Цифра 6% относится только к купленным в кассе билетам, не ко всей помощи. Успешные 94% учитывают лишь начатые покупки; ушедшие до начала не вошли в расчёт. Испытание также проходило вне самого загруженного праздничного периода. Эти ограничения не доказывают, что автоматы не справятся, но не позволяют считать полноценную замену уже подтверждённой.

Из заявленных 420 тысяч долларов годовой экономии нужно вычесть 110 тысяч на удалённую поддержку. Оставшиеся 310 тысяч — ещё не окончательная чистая выгода: дополнительную работу сотрудников на платформах пока не оценили. Если независимая проверка, график поддержки, помощь при сбоях и полное сравнение стоимости покажут работоспособность замены, условное закрытие можно рассматривать. При этом нельзя требовать отсутствия любого риска: у нынешних касс тоже бывают недостатки. После изменения нужно учитывать незавершённые попытки, нерешённые обращения и нагрузку на персонал, сохранив возможность усилить очную помощь. До голосования остаётся шесть недель; если необходимых ответов не будет, редакция предлагает перенести решение.

Label $420,000 as gross annual savings and $310,000 as the amount remaining after quoted remote-support costs, before uncosted transferred work. Label 94% as completion among users who started a purchase, not all passengers needing assistance.
tasks.explanation: Разные форматы должны сохранять единицы, знаменатели и условие рекомендации.

transfer.prompt: A university closes a help desk because 97% of submitted forms are processed online; abandoned forms and informal advice are uncounted. Gross savings exclude outsourced chat costs. Write a 250–350-word editorial with a real counterargument, a decision threshold and a satirical sentence that does not invent facts.
transfer.model:
A form can pass through an online system successfully while the person unable to submit it disappears from the success rate. The university’s figure of 97 percent is useful information about submitted forms, but it cannot settle the future of the help desk. It leaves abandoned attempts and informal advice outside the count. A system should not earn full marks simply by making the difficult questions statistically invisible.

That is an argument for a fuller evaluation, not a permanent defense of the counter. Digital services may reduce waiting, make routine transactions easier and spare users an uncomfortable encounter. Keeping a desk also consumes resources that might improve support elsewhere. A serious case against closure must therefore explain which work needs to survive, not assume that every existing arrangement deserves protection.

Before treating closure as permanent, the university should publish a cost comparison that subtracts outsourced chat costs from the proposed gross savings. No amount is supplied here, so neither the size of the net saving nor its disappearance can honestly be announced. The evaluation should also examine why users abandon forms, which questions are resolved informally and whether the proposed alternatives can handle those needs.

I would accept closure if that evidence shows a workable replacement with clear responsibility for unresolved requests and support that people can actually reach. The threshold should concern foreseeable needs, rather than demand a perfect service or zero risk. If the desk has already closed, the same conditions should determine whether additional support must be restored. After a change, the university should monitor abandoned attempts, unresolved cases and demand transferred to other staff. A route to correct the arrangement matters as much as the confidence of the launch announcement. Processing a form is a result; helping someone complete the process is the larger service the decision must evaluate.
transfer.explanation: Перенос требует новой сатиры и нового объёма помощи, а не замены station на university.

materials.title: Письменные материалы
materials.text:
INQUIRY DOSSIER — original fictional material, not legal advice.
A cultural center commissioned an internal review after a public event was canceled twenty minutes before opening because its temporary stage had not received the venue’s required sign-off. The written procedure says that the production manager must submit a completed inspection checklist to the venue officer by noon on the event day. The venue officer must then confirm acceptance or identify missing items. An email at 11:42 from the production manager attaches a checklist with the lighting section blank and says, “Everything else is ready; lighting confirmation follows shortly.” At 12:06 the venue officer replies, “Received, thank you. We will proceed on that basis.” The officer later says “received” acknowledged delivery, not approval; the manager says “proceed” reasonably indicated permission to continue preparations. Neither email explicitly states that sign-off has been granted.
At 2:10, a lighting contractor sends a message to a separate supplier group: “All set here.” The contractor says this referred to equipment installation, not the venue checklist. The production manager was not in that group. A volunteer coordinator saw a screenshot at 2:35 but did not forward it, believing the professionals were already communicating. At 4:40, the venue officer notices that the lighting section is still incomplete. The event is due to open at five. The officer asks for confirmation, but the contractor has left to collect another item and cannot be reached immediately. The center cancels at 4:40 rather than admit the audience without sign-off. No injury occurred. The review has no evidence that the stage was physically unsafe; it also lacks the completed inspection needed to establish that the required check occurred.
An early management summary calls the cancellation “a supplier communication failure.” Staff representatives object that this assigns the problem outside the center before examining its procedure. The contractor objects to being described as having certified safety in the “all set” message. The director worries that a report emphasizing ambiguity will avoid accountability. The review’s remit is to establish a defensible account of the process, identify contributing conditions and recommend improvements. It is not authorized to determine legal liability, discipline individuals or make findings about physical safety beyond the evidence.
The center has complete copies of the emails but only the supplied screenshot from the supplier group. There is no recording of a reported midday phone call in which the manager recalls asking whether anything remained outstanding. The venue officer does not remember that call. Both agree that no written final approval was issued. The system contains a status field called “received,” but no separate field for “complete and accepted.” Staff have sometimes used green highlighting to mean ready, although the procedure does not define it. The director wants a concise public account and a more detailed internal finding that can guide action without making uncertainty an excuse for inaction.
materials.source: Авторский вымышленный материал English Workshop, 2026

materials.title: Сообщение / разговор
materials.text: Director: If nobody clearly approved the stage, surely the manager simply failed to do the job. Reviewer: The checklist remained incomplete, and the manager had a defined submission responsibility. We should state that. We also need to examine why the venue’s reply suggested proceeding without identifying the missing section. Venue officer: I never said it was approved. Staff representative: The absence of that word matters, but it doesn't erase the effect of “we will proceed on that basis.” Contractor: And “all set here” was about installation. I was not issuing the venue’s acceptance. Reviewer: Agreed. We should attribute each phrase to its channel and task rather than merge them into an approval nobody actually gave. Director: I do not want a report that says everyone misunderstood and therefore nobody is responsible. Reviewer: Responsibility can be specific even where motive and memory remain uncertain. The production submission was incomplete; the acceptance status was not explicitly resolved; the process lacked a shared final state and a timely escalation point. We can recommend owners for those actions without deciding whose account of an unrecorded call is true. Staff representative: Nor should the absence of injury be used to suggest the missing inspection was unimportant. Contractor: But don't imply the stage was unsafe simply because the paperwork was missing. Reviewer: Exactly. The evidence supports a failure to establish the required sign-off, not either of those stronger conclusions. Director: Then give me language that the public can understand without publishing every contested recollection.
materials.source: Авторский сценарий для синтезированной озвучки English Workshop, 2026

rubric: Хронология и статусы доказательств точны.
Прагматическое значение фраз связано с каналом и полномочиями.
Ответственность конкретна при честно сохранённой неопределённости.
Рекомендация меняет координацию, а публичное сообщение не превышает установленное.

tasks.prompt: Construct a precise chronology and distinguish a failed procedure, an inference about interpretation and an unresolved factual claim. Explain what the absence of injury and the missing checklist do—and do not—show.
tasks.model: At 11:42 an incomplete checklist was submitted; at 12:06 the venue acknowledged it with ambiguous language about proceeding. The 2:10 supplier message concerned installation in another channel; a volunteer saw it at 2:35. At 4:40 the missing section was identified and the event canceled. The incomplete submission and absent written approval are documented. The manager’s interpretation of “proceed” is plausible but not explicit authorization. The midday call remains unresolved. No injury does not validate the process, while missing sign-off does not prove physical danger.
tasks.explanation: C2 требует калибровать каждый отдельный вывод; общий ярлык communication failure слишком груб.

tasks.prompt: Explain how the reviewer avoids both individual blame unsupported by evidence and diffuse responsibility. Analyze why “all set here” cannot be treated as a portable approval statement.
tasks.model: The reviewer identifies specific responsibilities and failures—complete submission, explicit acceptance and escalation—without deciding disputed memory or motive. “All set here” is indexical: its meaning depends on the supplier channel, installation task and speaker’s authority. Moving it into the venue approval process changes its apparent force without evidence that the contractor intended or could grant that approval.
tasks.explanation: Разбор прагматики должен связать here, канал, задачу и полномочия, а не просто назвать фразу двусмысленной.

tasks.prompt: Write a 330–430-word internal finding and a 120–160-word public account. Separate findings, interpretation and unresolved matters; assign actionable owners; give a recommendation that improves real coordination rather than only adding paperwork. Respect the review’s remit and avoid hindsight certainty.
tasks.model:
INTERNAL FINDING: The event was canceled because the venue’s required sign-off had not been established before opening. The documented record shows that the production manager submitted a checklist at 11:42 with the lighting section incomplete. The venue officer’s 12:06 reply acknowledged receipt and used the phrase “we will proceed on that basis,” but did not explicitly grant acceptance or identify the outstanding section. Both parties agree that no written final approval followed. The manager’s reading of “proceed” as permission to continue preparations is understandable; it is not equivalent to evidence that the venue accepted the completed inspection. The contractor’s later “all set here” message appeared in a separate supplier channel and is attributed to equipment installation. It should not be recast as venue approval. The alleged midday call remains unresolved because there is no recording and recollections differ.
These limits do not prevent specific findings about responsibility. The production manager retained responsibility for completing the submission. The venue’s response failed to make the outstanding acceptance state explicit, and the process did not provide a shared final status or an early escalation point. The system’s single “received” field and informal use of green highlighting made it easier to conflate delivery, completion and acceptance. The volunteer’s decision not to forward a screenshot belongs in the chronology but should not be treated as the missing formal approval or the sole cause of cancellation. The evidence establishes a failure to demonstrate the required inspection and acceptance. It does not establish physical unsafety, and the absence of injury does not establish that the process was adequate.
The production lead should own a complete submission with named outstanding items and deadlines. The venue officer should own an explicit accepted-or-incomplete response, using a shared status visible to both teams. A designated event lead should review unresolved items at a scheduled point early enough to obtain confirmation, with a direct escalation route and authority to pause preparations. These changes should be rehearsed with a realistic incomplete-checklist scenario, testing whether staff can identify who must act and whether a supplier update changes the formal state. Success should be measured by resolved responsibilities and timely decisions, not additional completed fields alone. Questions of legal liability or discipline fall outside this review.

PUBLIC ACCOUNT: The event was canceled because the required stage sign-off had not been confirmed before opening. Our review found an incomplete checklist and communications that did not clearly distinguish receipt from final acceptance. A later supplier message concerned installation and did not provide the missing venue approval. We have not established that the stage was physically unsafe, but we also did not have the completed check required to proceed. We are assigning clear responsibility for complete submissions and explicit acceptance, introducing a shared status and an earlier escalation point, and testing those arrangements in practice. Some recollections remain disputed; the documented process failures are sufficient to require action. We are sorry for the disruption to the audience and participants and will communicate confirmed changes clearly.
tasks.explanation: Внутренний текст называет владельцев действий и границы; публичный сохраняет существенную неопределённость без детализации спорного звонка.

tasks.prompt: Record a 3–4-minute briefing. Director: “This sounds like nobody is accountable.” State differentiated responsibility and one limit. Contractor: “Remove us entirely; our message was irrelevant.” Explain why the message belongs in the chronology but not as approval. End by negotiating a public sentence that neither overstates nor conceals the finding.
tasks.model:
The report does assign responsibility. The production manager had to submit a completed checklist, and the lighting section remained blank. The venue officer then needed to confirm acceptance or identify missing items. The reply acknowledged receipt and used language about proceeding without explicitly resolving the outstanding section. Those are different responsibilities; describing both does not mean that neither matters.

There is also a process responsibility. The system offered a received status without a separate complete-and-accepted state. Informal green highlighting did not have a defined meaning. We should assign an event lead to check unresolved items early enough for someone to act, with an escalation route and a visible final status. Adding another box would be inadequate if people still could not tell who had to make the next decision.

The limit is equally specific. We cannot decide whose memory of an unrecorded phone call is correct on the supplied record, or use that dispute to determine motive. Legal liability and discipline are outside this review. Nor does an incomplete checklist prove that the stage was physically unsafe. It proves that the required inspection and acceptance had not been established. The absence of an injury does not repair that failure.

To the contractor, I accept that “all set here” was not venue sign-off. Its channel and described installation purpose must remain attached to the quotation. I would remove any wording that presents it as your certification of safety or permission to admit the audience. However, I would not remove the message from the chronology. A volunteer saw the screenshot and believed that the professionals were already communicating. That helps explain the information available around the event, even though it could not complete the venue process.

The distinction allows us to acknowledge the message without making it the sole cause of cancellation. We should test the revised procedure using a similar incomplete-checklist situation: can staff identify the unresolved requirement, the responsible person and the point at which preparations must pause? That test examines coordination rather than the appearance of complete records.

For the public account, I propose: “The required approval was not established because an incomplete submission and ambiguous status communications were not resolved in time; a supplier message about installation did not provide the missing venue sign-off.” Could we agree on that sentence, followed by the specific responsibilities we are changing and the limits of what this review can establish?
tasks.explanation: Устный синтез сохраняет причинную значимость сообщения без подмены его речевого действия.

tasks.prompt: Write a 140–190-word Russian briefing for volunteers and a concise English implementation checklist expressed as sentences, not vague labels. Explain what a screenshot can and cannot authorize.
tasks.model:
Отмена произошла потому, что до открытия не было подтверждено обязательное согласование сцены. Чек-лист оставался неполным, а сообщение «получено, продолжаем» не отделяло получение от окончательного принятия. Скриншот поставщика относился к монтажу и сам по себе не мог разрешить открытие. При этом его не нужно удалять из истории: координатор видел сообщение и считал, что специалисты уже общаются. Важно сохранять контекст, а не превращать скриншот в разрешение от площадки.

Это не доказывает, что сцена была опасна, но отсутствие происшествия тоже не заменяет обязательную проверку. Воспоминания о телефонном разговоре расходятся; комиссия не устанавливает юридическую ответственность и не назначает наказания. Для волонтёров предлагается понятный порядок: видеть официальный статус, знать ответственного за неясность и передавать вопрос достаточно рано. Не надо самостоятельно толковать зелёную отметку или чужую переписку. Производственная команда должна завершить документ, площадка — явно принять его или назвать недостающее, руководитель мероприятия — организовать своевременное уточнение. Эти обязанности следует проверить в учебной ситуации, чтобы новые поля действительно помогали действовать.

Production must submit a complete checklist or name each outstanding item. The venue must explicitly record acceptance or incompleteness. The event lead must escalate unresolved items before the agreed cutoff; screenshots may inform the review but do not change acceptance status by themselves.

transfer.prompt: A publishing team releases a report after “looks fine to me” appears in a design chat, while the factual-review section is blank. No false claim has yet been identified. The author recalls an unrecorded approval call; the reviewer disputes it. Write an internal finding and public correction note that distinguish layout approval, factual verification, absence of detected error and unresolved memory.
transfer.model:
INTERNAL FINDING: The report was released while the factual-review section remained blank. The design-chat phrase “looks fine to me” does not establish completed factual verification; its channel and wording need to be kept distinct from explicit release approval. The author recalls an approval call, but the reviewer disputes it and no recording is supplied. That disagreement remains unresolved. No false claim has yet been identified, which is different from confirmation that all claims were checked. I recommend assigning the factual reviewer to record completed checks and outstanding questions, and a release owner to confirm the final state before further promotion of the report. Any corrected version should identify actual changes rather than imply that an error has already been found.

PUBLIC NOTE: The report was released before its factual-review status was clearly recorded. We are checking that status and the supporting claims. No false statement has yet been identified, but that does not establish that verification was complete. The design-chat comment was not a clear record of factual approval. We will distinguish any confirmed correction from changes to the review process when we report the findings.
transfer.explanation: Новый речевой акт и иной риск проверяют перенос прагматического анализа и соразмерного вывода.
